messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mr. Kwame Osei is a 77-year-old married man of Ghanaian heritage who worked as a school principal for over four decades before retiring last year. He sits in the clinic with his hands folded, his voice steady but his eyes darting to the window every few seconds. Three years ago, he was assaulted outside the school where he had worked for thirty years. It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn; he had stayed late to prepare for a parent-teacher conference, and as he walked toward his car, a man emerged from behind the dumpster near the parking lot. The man smelled strongly of cheap whiskey and demanded Kwame's wallet. When Kwame hesitated, reaching slowly into his pocket, the man shoved him against the brick wall and hit him twice across the face with a metal pipe. Kwame lost consciousness briefly, and when he came to, the man was gone, along with his wallet and the gold ring his father had given him decades ago. What stayed with him most vividly, though, was not the physical pain but the smell—that thick, sour alcohol odor that he can still summon in his nostrils without warning, and the sickening realization that he had been utterly powerless, forced to comply while someone else controlled every second of what happened to him.

In the months that followed, Kwame found himself unable to walk past the school building without his chest tightening. The smell of alcohol—even a guest at a family gathering holding a glass of wine—would send him into a state of hypervigilance that he could not shake. He began scanning every room he entered for exits, a habit that became so automatic that he would sometimes find himself mapping escape routes in his own living room. A sudden movement from his wife reaching for a cup would make him flinch, his heart hammering as if the assailant had reappeared, and he would feel a flash of grief so sharp that it took his breath away—grief not just for the lost ring or the lost sense of safety, but for the man he used to be, the one who walked through the world without looking over his shoulder. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like truth, that the assault had happened because of the way he acted. He should have just handed over the wallet immediately. He should have been faster, smarter, more decisive. He could not rely on himself anymore—his own judgment had failed him when it mattered most, and this thought surfaced every time he caught a whiff of alcohol or felt that familiar loss of control creeping in.

The memory of the assault did not stay neatly in the past. Sometimes, when he was sitting quietly, he would hear the man's voice in his head—the growled demand for his wallet, the scrape of shoes on asphalt—and he would feel nothing at all, as if he were watching a movie about someone else's life. This emotional numbness frightened him more than the fear did, because it made him wonder if he had already died inside. Other times, the memory would surge back unbidden when he least expected it, triggered by the scent of beer on a stranger's breath as he walked down the street, and he would feel the overwhelming grief all over again, as fresh as the night it happened. He started avoiding crowds, then avoided leaving the house altogether except for essential errands, and even those he planned with military precision. He told himself he was being careful, but he knew, somewhere underneath, that he was hiding. The scanning for exits, the startle response to unexpected movement, the way his body braced for danger every time he heard footsteps behind him—all of it reinforced his belief that he could not trust the world, could not trust other people to keep him safe, and above all could not trust himself to handle even ordinary situations without freezing or failing.

His wife noticed that he had stopped attending their weekly church service, something that had been central to his identity for his entire adult life. When she asked why, he said he was tired, but the real reason was that the church's fellowship hall always smelled of the wine used for communion, and the close quarters of the pews made him feel trapped. He could not explain this to her without admitting how broken he felt, and so he simply withdrew further, each retreat deepening his conviction that he was no longer the man she had married. The more he avoided, the more he ruminated on his failure to act decisively during the assault, and the more he ruminated, the more he scanned for exits and startled at shadows, which in turn brought the memory roaring back with its accompanying grief and numbness. The loop tightened month by month, until he was spending most of his days in his armchair, watching the street from behind the curtain, certain that danger was always just outside.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment of collapse. Last week, his grandson—a boy of ten—came to visit and accidentally knocked over a bottle of cologne in the bathroom. The sharp alcoholic scent hit Kwame's nostrils before he could prepare himself, and he found himself on the kitchen floor, shaking, unable to speak, while his wife called the paramedics. He was not physically hurt, but the humiliation of being seen that way, of being so utterly unmanned by a smell, broke something open in him. He is afraid of what he has become—afraid that he will never feel safe again, afraid that he has lost himself completely, and afraid, most of all, that the man who survived the assault is not the same man who can survive its aftermath. He is hoping, quietly, that someone can help him find his way back.
